name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_DIAGRAM_Q01 - Classification of open closed and isolated systems

questiontext.text:
Three thermodynamic systems (I), (II), and (III) are shown below, where arrows indicate the possible exchange of matter and energy across the system boundary with the surroundings.

Which of the following correctly identifies systems (I), (II), and (III)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows three containers: (I) has an open top with conducting walls allowing both matter and energy exchange; (II) is sealed with conducting walls allowing only energy exchange; (III) is sealed with insulated walls allowing neither matter nor energy exchange.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Thermodynamic systems are classified strictly by whether matter and energy can cross the boundary between the system and its surroundings.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- Open system: exchange of both energy and matter.
- Closed system: exchange of energy only, no exchange of matter.
- Isolated system: no exchange of either energy or matter.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
System (I) exchanges both matter and energy with the surroundings, so it is an open system. System (II) exchanges energy through its conducting walls while preventing matter transfer, so it is a closed system. System (III) has sealed insulated walls preventing both matter and energy exchange, so it is an isolated system.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Matching the three definitions confirms that (I) is an open system, (II) is a closed system, and (III) is an isolated system.

answer.text: (I) Closed system, (II) Open system, (III) Isolated system
(I) Open system, (II) Closed system, (III) Isolated system
(I) Open system, (II) Isolated system, (III) Closed system
(I) Isolated system, (II) Closed system, (III) Open system

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_DIAGRAM_Q02 - Extensive and intensive properties by partitioning

questiontext.text:
A gas is enclosed in a container of volume \(V\) at temperature \(T\) as shown in the left diagram. A thin partition is then inserted to divide the container into two equal compartments, as shown in the right diagram.

What conclusion about thermodynamic properties is directly illustrated by this diagram?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Initially, the gas occupies volume \(V\) at temperature \(T\). After inserting a partition in the middle, each compartment has volume \(\frac{V}{2}\) while the temperature remains \(T\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
The gas is uniform throughout the container before and after inserting the partition, and thermal equilibrium is maintained.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
An extensive property depends on the quantity or size of matter present in the system, whereas an intensive property does not depend on the quantity or size of matter present.

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Halving the amount of gas in each compartment halves the volume from \(V\) to \(\frac{V}{2}\), showing that volume depends on the size of the system (extensive property). In contrast, the temperature \(T\) remains unchanged in both halves, showing that temperature is independent of the amount of matter (intensive property).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, the diagram illustrates that volume is an extensive property and temperature is an intensive property.

answer.text: Both volume and temperature are extensive properties.
Both volume and temperature are intensive properties.
Volume is an intensive property and temperature is an extensive property.
Volume is an extensive property and temperature is an intensive property.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_DIAGRAM_Q03 - Work done in single step compression from pV plot

questiontext.text:
An ideal gas in a cylinder fitted with a frictionless piston is compressed in a single step from an initial volume \(V_i = 10\text{ L}\) to a final volume \(V_f = 4\text{ L}\) by a constant external pressure \(p_{\mathrm{ex}} = 2\text{ atm}\), as represented in the \(p\text{-}V\) diagram below.

What is the work done \(w\) on the gas during this compression?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the \(p\text{-}V\) diagram, constant external pressure \(p_{\mathrm{ex}} = 2\text{ atm}\), initial volume \(V_i = 10\text{ L}\), and final volume \(V_f = 4\text{ L}\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
By IUPAC sign convention in chemical thermodynamics, work done on the system during compression is positive, and work done by the system during expansion is negative.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
For a single-step irreversible process against constant external pressure \(p_{\mathrm{ex}}\):
\[w = -p_{\mathrm{ex}}\Delta V = -p_{\mathrm{ex}}(V_f - V_i)\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Calculate \(\Delta V\):
\[\Delta V = V_f - V_i = 4\text{ L} - 10\text{ L} = -6\text{ L}\]
Substitute \(p_{\mathrm{ex}}\) and \(\Delta V\) into the work equation:
\[w = -(2\text{ atm}) \times (-6\text{ L}) = +12\text{ L}\cdot\text{atm}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The positive sign confirms that work is done on the gas during compression, and the magnitude equals the shaded area \(2\text{ atm} \times 6\text{ L} = 12\text{ L}\cdot\text{atm}\). Thus, \(w = +12\text{ L}\cdot\text{atm}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_DIAGRAM_Q04 - Reversible versus finite step compression pV plots

questiontext.text:
The two \(p\text{-}V\) plots below show the compression of an ideal gas from initial volume \(V_i\) to final volume \(V_f\) at constant temperature: Plot X shows compression in finite steps, while Plot Y shows compression in infinite infinitesimal steps.

Which of the following statements is correct regarding Plot X and Plot Y?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Both \(p\text{-}V\) plots depict isothermal compression of an ideal gas from \(V_i\) to \(V_f\). Plot X consists of finite-step rectangles above the isotherm, while Plot Y is bounded by the smooth \(p\text{-}V\) curve.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Work done on the gas during compression is positive and equals the shaded area under the \(p_{\mathrm{ex}}\text{-}V\) path.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
- For finite-step irreversible compression: \(w_{\mathrm{irrev}} = -\sum p_{\mathrm{ex}}\Delta V\).
- For infinite-step reversible compression: \(w_{\mathrm{rev}} = -\int_{V_i}^{V_f} p_{\mathrm{in}}\,dV = -2.303\,nRT\log\frac{V_f}{V_i}\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
In Plot X, the external pressure changes in finite steps, representing an irreversible process where the rectangular areas extend above the smooth equilibrium curve. In Plot Y, \(p_{\mathrm{ex}} = p_{\mathrm{in}} + dp\) at every stage, so the process proceeds infinitely slowly through equilibrium states, representing a reversible process. Comparing the shaded areas shows that the area in Plot X is greater than the area under the curve in Plot Y.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, Plot Y represents a reversible compression, and the magnitude of work done on the gas in Plot X is greater than that in Plot Y.

answer.text: Plot X represents a reversible process, and the work done on the gas is less in Plot X than in Plot Y.
Both Plot X and Plot Y represent reversible processes with identical work done on the gas.
Plot Y represents a reversible process, and the magnitude of work done on the gas is greater in Plot X than in Plot Y.
Plot Y represents an irreversible process, and the work done on the gas is zero in both plots.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_DIAGRAM_Q05 - Measurement of internal energy change in bomb calorimeter

questiontext.text:
The schematic diagram below represents a sealed steel vessel immersed in a water bath used to measure the heat of combustion of a sample in excess dioxygen.

Which thermodynamic quantity is directly determined from the temperature rise \(\Delta T\) measured in this apparatus?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
The diagram shows a bomb calorimeter containing a sealed steel vessel (bomb) immersed in a water bath with a stirrer and thermometer.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Because the steel bomb is rigid and sealed, the reaction occurs at constant volume (\(\Delta V = 0\)) and no heat escapes to the surroundings outside the calorimeter.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. Pressure-volume work: \(w = -p_{\mathrm{ex}}\Delta V\).
2. First law of thermodynamics: \(\Delta U = q + w\).
3. Heat exchange: \(q_v = -C_v\Delta T\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since the volume of the sealed bomb does not change (\(\Delta V = 0\)), the pressure-volume work done is \(w = -p_{\mathrm{ex}}(0) = 0\), even when gases are involved. Substituting \(w = 0\) into the first law gives \(\Delta U = q_v\). Using the known heat capacity \(C_v\) of the calorimeter and the measured temperature rise \(\Delta T\), the heat evolved by the reaction at constant volume is \(q_v = -C_v\Delta T = \Delta U\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Hence, a bomb calorimeter directly measures the internal energy change \(\Delta U\) of the reaction at constant volume.

answer.text: Internal energy change \(\Delta U\) at constant volume
Gibbs free energy change \(\Delta G\) at constant temperature

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_DIAGRAM_Q06 - Enthalpy diagram for endothermic chemical reaction

questiontext.text:
Consider the enthalpy diagram shown below for a chemical reaction proceeding from reactants to products.

Which of the following statements and example reactions correctly matches this enthalpy diagram?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
In the enthalpy diagram, the total enthalpy of products \(H_p\) lies higher than the total enthalpy of reactants \(H_r\) (\(H_p > H_r\)), and the vertical arrow for \(\Delta_r H\) points upward from \(H_r\) to \(H_p\).

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
At constant pressure, \(\Delta_r H = H_p - H_r = q_p\). A positive \(\Delta_r H\) indicates an endothermic reaction (heat absorbed from the surroundings), and a negative \(\Delta_r H\) indicates an exothermic reaction.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\(\Delta_r H = \sum H_{\text{products}} - \sum H_{\text{reactants}} = H_p - H_r\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since \(H_p > H_r\), \(\Delta_r H = H_p - H_r > 0\), which corresponds to an endothermic reaction where net heat is absorbed from the surroundings. Among common textbook examples, \(\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{N_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NO_2(g)}\) has \(\Delta_r H^\ominus = +33.2\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) (endothermic), whereas combustion and ammonia synthesis are exothermic (\(\Delta_r H^\ominus < 0\)).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Therefore, the diagram represents an endothermic reaction with \(\Delta_r H > 0\), such as \(\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{N_2(g)} + \mathrm{O_2(g)} \rightarrow \mathrm{NO_2(g)}\).

questiontext.text:
The thermochemical cycle below illustrates the conversion of state A to state B directly and via intermediate states C and D.

Using Hess's law of constant heat summation, what is the value of \(\Delta_r H_3\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the thermochemical cycle:
- Direct path \(\mathrm{A \rightarrow B}\): \(\Delta_r H = -200\text{ kJ}\).
- Multi-step path \(\mathrm{A \rightarrow C \rightarrow D \rightarrow B}\): \(\Delta_r H_1 = -120\text{ kJ}\), \(\Delta_r H_2 = +45\text{ kJ}\), and \(\Delta_r H_3\) is unknown.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
All steps occur at the same temperature and pressure. Since enthalpy \(H\) is a state function, \(\Delta_r H\) depends only on the initial state A and final state B.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Hess's law of constant heat summation:
\[\Delta_r H = \Delta_r H_1 + \Delta_r H_2 + \Delta_r H_3\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values into Hess's law equation:
\[-200\text{ kJ} = (-120\text{ kJ}) + (+45\text{ kJ}) + \Delta_r H_3\]
\[-200\text{ kJ} = -75\text{ kJ} + \Delta_r H_3\]
\[\Delta_r H_3 = -200\text{ kJ} + 75\text{ kJ} = -125\text{ kJ}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Summing the multi-step path gives \(-120 + 45 + (-125) = -200\text{ kJ}\), matching the direct path \(\Delta_r H\). Thus, \(\Delta_r H_3 = -125\text{ kJ}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_DIAGRAM_Q08 - Born-Haber cycle lattice enthalpy of sodium chloride

questiontext.text:
The Born-Haber enthalpy diagram for \(\mathrm{NaCl(s)}\) is shown below with standard enthalpy values (in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)) at \(298\text{ K}\).

From the Born-Haber cycle, what is the lattice enthalpy \(\Delta_{\mathrm{lattice}}H^\ominus\) for the dissociation \(\mathrm{NaCl(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^+(g)} + \mathrm{Cl^-(g)}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the Born-Haber diagram at \(298\text{ K}\) (all values in \(\text{kJ mol}^{-1}\)):
- \(\Delta_f H^\ominus[\mathrm{NaCl(s)}] = -411.2\)
- \(\Delta_{\mathrm{sub}} H^\ominus[\mathrm{Na(s)}] = +108.4\)
- \(\Delta_i H^\ominus[\mathrm{Na(g)}] = +496.0\)
- \(\frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\mathrm{bond}} H^\ominus[\mathrm{Cl_2(g)}] = +121.0\)
- \(\Delta_{\mathrm{eg}} H^\ominus[\mathrm{Cl(g)}] = -348.6\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Lattice enthalpy \(\Delta_{\mathrm{lattice}}H^\ominus\) is defined as the enthalpy change when \(1\text{ mol}\) of an ionic crystal dissociates into gaseous ions: \(\mathrm{NaCl(s)} \rightarrow \mathrm{Na^+(g)} + \mathrm{Cl^-(g)}\), which is endothermic (positive).

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
By Hess's law, the sum of enthalpy changes around the Born-Haber cycle is zero:
\[\Delta_{\mathrm{lattice}}H^\ominus = -\Delta_f H^\ominus + \Delta_{\mathrm{sub}}H^\ominus + \Delta_i H^\ominus + \frac{1}{2}\Delta_{\mathrm{bond}}H^\ominus + \Delta_{\mathrm{eg}}H^\ominus\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute each value into the equation:
\[\Delta_{\mathrm{lattice}}H^\ominus = -(-411.2) + 108.4 + 496.0 + 121.0 + (-348.6)\]
\[\Delta_{\mathrm{lattice}}H^\ominus = 411.2 + 108.4 + 496.0 + 121.0 - 348.6\]
\[\Delta_{\mathrm{lattice}}H^\ominus = 1136.6 - 348.6 = +788.0\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
Dissociation of \(\mathrm{NaCl(s)}\) into gaseous ions requires overcoming strong electrostatic attractions, so a large positive value of \(+788\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) is physically consistent. Thus, \(\Delta_{\mathrm{lattice}}H^\ominus = +788\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\).

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_DIAGRAM_Q09 - Enthalpy of solution from lattice and hydration enthalpies

questiontext.text:
The enthalpy cycle for dissolving \(1\text{ mol}\) of an ionic compound \(\mathrm{AB(s)}\) in water is shown below.

What is the standard enthalpy of solution \(\Delta_{\mathrm{sol}}H^\ominus\) of \(\mathrm{AB(s)}\), and how is its solubility in water expected to change with a rise in temperature?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
From the enthalpy cycle for \(\mathrm{AB(s)}\):
- Lattice enthalpy: \(\Delta_{\mathrm{lattice}}H^\ominus = +788\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)
- Hydration enthalpy: \(\Delta_{\mathrm{hyd}}H^\ominus = -784\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\)

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
Dissolution is represented as a two-step Hess's law cycle: dissociation of the solid lattice into gaseous ions followed by hydration of the gaseous ions.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
\[\Delta_{\mathrm{sol}}H^\ominus = \Delta_{\mathrm{lattice}}H^\ominus + \Delta_{\mathrm{hyd}}H^\ominus\]

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Substitute the given values:
\[\Delta_{\mathrm{sol}}H^\ominus = (+788\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}) + (-784\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}) = +4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\]
Because \(\Delta_{\mathrm{sol}}H^\ominus = +4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1} > 0\), the dissolution of \(\mathrm{AB(s)}\) is endothermic. For endothermic dissolution processes, solubility increases with a rise in temperature.

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
The positive value \(+4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\) confirms an endothermic dissolution accompanied by a small heat absorption, so solubility increases as temperature rises.

answer.text: \(\Delta_{\mathrm{sol}}H^\ominus = -4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); solubility decreases with rise in temperature.
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{sol}}H^\ominus = +4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); solubility increases with rise in temperature.
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{sol}}H^\ominus = +1572\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); solubility decreases with rise in temperature.
\(\Delta_{\mathrm{sol}}H^\ominus = +4\text{ kJ mol}^{-1}\); solubility decreases with rise in temperature.

name.text: NEET_UG_CHEMISTRY_THERMODYNAMICS_DIAGRAM_Q10 - Spontaneous diffusion of gases in an isolated system

questiontext.text:
Two ideal gases A (black circles) and B (white circles) at the same temperature are placed in an isolated container separated by a partition (State I). When the partition is removed, the gases spontaneously diffuse into each other to form a uniform mixture (State II).

For this spontaneous mixing process in an isolated system, what are the correct signs of \(\Delta U\), \(\Delta H\), and \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{total}}\)?

generalfeedback.text:
Step 1: Given Data and Conditions
Two ideal gases A and B at the same temperature are mixed in an isolated container (\(\text{no heat or work exchange with surroundings}\)) by removing a partition.

Step 2: Assumptions and Sign Conventions
For an isolated system, \(q = 0\) and \(w = 0\). For ideal gases at constant temperature, internal energy \(U\) and enthalpy \(H\) depend only on temperature.

Step 3: Relevant Formulae and Principles
1. First law of thermodynamics: \(\Delta U = q + w\).
2. Second law of thermodynamics for a spontaneous process: \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{total}} = \Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}} + \Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}} > 0\).

Step 4: Step-by-Step Working
Since the system is isolated, \(q = 0\) and \(w = 0\), giving \(\Delta U = 0\). Because the temperature of the ideal gases remains constant and there are no intermolecular interactions, \(\Delta H = 0\) as well. Before removing the partition, gas A is confined to the left half and gas B to the right half; after removing the partition, both gases occupy the entire volume, making the distribution more disordered and less predictable. Thus, the entropy of the system increases (\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{sys}} > 0\)) while \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{surr}} = 0\), so \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{total}} > 0\).

Step 5: Check and Final Answer
This confirms that enthalpy change is not the driving force here (\(\Delta H = 0\)); instead, the increase in entropy (\(\Delta S_{\mathrm{total}} > 0\)) drives the spontaneous mixing. Therefore, \(\Delta U = 0\), \(\Delta H = 0\), and \(\Delta S_{\mathrm{total}} > 0\).
